title: What is the practical difference between Minor GC, Major GC, and Full GC, and why does G1 not really have a "Major GC"?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Minor, Major, and Full GC?

s1_definition.profdef: A Minor GC collects only the Young generation and is frequent and cheap. A Major GC, in the classic terminology, collects the Old generation. A Full GC collects the entire heap, Young plus Old, and usually Metaspace, and it is the most expensive. In practice the terms Major and Full are often used interchangeably in the older generational collectors because an old-space collection there effectively involved the whole heap. The G1 collector breaks this neat picture: it divides the heap into many small regions and reclaims old-generation garbage incrementally through concurrent marking plus mixed collections that clean young and selected old regions together, so there is no single monolithic "Major GC" phase; a true Full GC in G1 is only a rare fallback.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a Minor GC is a quick tidy of the busy front counter while tellers keep working. A Major GC is a cleanup of the deep archive room. A Full GC is locking the whole building and auditing everything at once. In the old way of working, cleaning the archive basically meant halting the whole building, so people blurred "clean the archive" and "audit everything." G1 reorganizes the archive into many small labeled lockers and cleans just a handful of the fullest lockers during each quick tidy, so there is never one giant archive-wide shutdown; a full building audit only happens as an emergency fallback.
s1_definition.oneliner: Minor GC cleans the Young generation cheaply, Major GC cleans the Old generation, Full GC cleans the whole heap, and G1 has no distinct Major GC because it reclaims old regions incrementally via concurrent marking and mixed collections, reserving a true Full GC as a rare fallback.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Minor GC collects only the Young generation and is frequent and cheap. A Major GC, in the classic terminology, collects the Old generation. A Full GC collects the entire heap, Young plus Old, and usually Metaspace, and it is the most expensive. In practice the terms Major and Full are often used interchangeably in the older generational collectors because an old-space collection there effectively involved the whole heap. The G1 collector breaks this neat picture: it divides the heap into many small regions and reclaims old-generation garbage incrementally through concurrent marking plus mixed collections that clean young and selected old regions together, so there is no single monolithic "Major GC" phase; a true Full GC in G1 is only a rare fallback.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, a Minor GC is a quick tidy of the busy front counter while tellers keep working. A Major GC is a cleanup of the deep archive room. A Full GC is locking the whole building and auditing everything at once. In the old way of working, cleaning the archive basically meant halting the whole building, so people blurred "clean the archive" and "audit everything." G1 reorganizes the archive into many small labeled lockers and cleans just a handful of the fullest lockers during each quick tidy, so there is never one giant archive-wide shutdown; a full building audit only happens as an emergency fallback.

**One line to remember:** Minor GC cleans the Young generation cheaply, Major GC cleans the Old generation, Full GC cleans the whole heap, and G1 has no distinct Major GC because it reclaims old regions incrementally via concurrent marking and mixed collections, reserving a true Full GC as a rare fallback.

sections.s2_technical:
A Minor GC is a collection of the Young generation only: Eden and the Survivor spaces. It fires whenever Eden fills, it is a copying collection, and it is cheap because the cost is proportional to the small number of surviving objects. Minor GCs are still stop-the-world in most collectors, but their pauses are typically very short, on the order of milliseconds, because the young live set is small. A banking service under load may do many Minor GCs per second with negligible impact.

A Major GC, in the classic vocabulary of the older collectors like the Parallel or the CMS collector, refers to a collection of the Old generation, where long-lived, tenured objects reside. Reclaiming the Old generation is far more expensive than the Young generation because the Old generation is larger and its objects are long-lived, so more of them are actually live and must be traced and often compacted. The confusion is that in those classic collectors, collecting the Old generation generally required a stop-the-world pass over the whole heap, so a Major GC and a Full GC looked almost identical, and the terms got used interchangeably. Strictly, a Full GC collects the entire heap, both generations, and typically also unloads classes from Metaspace, so it is the broadest and most expensive event.

G1, the Garbage First collector and the default since Java 9, changes the model fundamentally. Instead of two large contiguous generations, G1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions, perhaps a couple of thousand of them, and labels each region at any moment as Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous for very large objects. A G1 young collection evacuates the young regions, just like a Minor GC. For old garbage, G1 does not do one giant Major GC. Instead it runs a concurrent marking cycle, mostly without stopping the application, to identify which old regions have the most garbage, and then it performs mixed collections, which are young collections that also evacuate a few of the most garbage-rich old regions at the same time. Because it only cleans the emptiest-of-live old regions each time, it spreads old-generation reclamation across many short pauses rather than one long one, which is the "Garbage First" idea: collect the regions that give the most free space for the least work.

So the reason G1 "does not really have a Major GC" is that there is no single dedicated stop-the-world phase that collects the entire Old generation at once. Old reclamation is incremental, concurrent for the marking part, and interleaved with young collections through mixed collections. A true Full GC still exists in G1, but it is a fallback that only happens when G1 cannot keep up, for example if the allocation rate outpaces concurrent marking and the heap fills before mixed collections can free enough space; that fallback is a slow, single-threaded or parallel whole-heap compaction and is treated as a sign of misconfiguration. The senior nuance is that modern collectors push this even further: ZGC and Shenandoah do essentially all of their work, including compaction, concurrently with the application, so they target sub-millisecond to low-single-digit-millisecond pauses even on very large heaps, which is why for a large-heap, low-latency banking service I would evaluate ZGC, while G1 remains an excellent balanced default.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's service was on an old collector and suffered occasional long pauses whenever the Old generation was collected, because a Major GC there was effectively a whole-heap stop-the-world event. This is exactly the classic Minor-versus-Major-versus-Full distinction, where young collections were cheap but old collections were painful.

Problem 2 — After switching to G1, the long single pause disappeared and old reclamation happened as many short mixed collections instead. This is exactly why G1 has no monolithic Major GC, because it cleans old regions incrementally alongside young collections.

In the mini-project we build a workload with both short-lived and long-lived objects, read every garbage-collector bean, and classify each as a young or old collector, reporting counts and pause times so the practical difference between the collection types is visible. The demo also prints which collector is active so the student can rerun under different collectors and compare.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/gctypes/GcTypesDemo.java

# G1 (default Java 9+): incremental old reclamation, no monolithic Major GC
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc* \
     -cp out com.bank.gctypes.GcTypesDemo

# Classic Parallel collector for contrast: distinct Young vs Full (old) collectors
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc* \
     -cp out com.bank.gctypes.GcTypesDemo

# ZGC for near-zero pause on large heaps
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc* -cp out com.bank.gctypes.GcTypesDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: fifty rounds, each allocating two hundred thousand short-lived ledger entries plus one retained sixty-four-kilobyte entry.

Step 1: The classifier prints the active collector names so the student knows whether G1, Parallel, or ZGC is running, and logs a baseline of young and old collection counts.

Step 2: Inside each round the inner loop creates two hundred thousand short-lived entries that die almost immediately. These fill Eden repeatedly and drive frequent Minor, or Young, collections, which are cheap and show up under the young collector counts.

Step 3: Each round also retains one larger entry in the list, so over fifty rounds a steadily growing set of long-lived objects accumulates and gets promoted to the Old generation.

Step 4: As the Old generation occupancy rises, old reclamation occurs. Under the classic Parallel collector this appears as a distinct full-heap collection counted under the old collector. Under G1 it appears as concurrent marking plus mixed collections, so there is no single big Major GC; the old-collector bean reflects G1's old-region work.

Step 5: The final report contrasts the cheap, frequent young collections against the fewer, costlier old collections, making the practical difference between Minor, Major, and Full concrete, and the collector name printed at the start explains why G1's behavior looks incremental rather than monolithic.

```text
[INFO] active collector: G1 Young Generation
[INFO] active collector: G1 Concurrent GC
[INFO] active collector: G1 Old Generation
[INFO] [startup] MINOR(young): count=0 time=0ms | MAJOR/FULL(old/mixed): count=0 time=0ms
[INFO] [after workload] MINOR(young): count=142 time=210ms | MAJOR/FULL(old/mixed): count=3 time=47ms
[INFO] retained long-lived entries = 50
[INFO] Young collectors = cheap Minor GCs; Old/mixed = Major/Full equivalent
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Classic generational collector (e.g. Parallel):
    Eden full ─→ MINOR GC (young only, cheap, frequent)
    Old full  ─→ MAJOR/FULL GC (whole heap, stop-the-world, costly)
                   └ Major ≈ Full here (old collection halts everything)

  G1 (region-based):
    heap = many regions [E][E][S][O][O][H]...
    young collection: evacuate Eden/Survivor regions (short pause)
    CONCURRENT MARKING (mostly no pause): find garbage-rich old regions
    MIXED collection: young regions + a FEW old regions together
       → old reclamation spread over many short pauses (no big Major GC)
    FULL GC: rare FALLBACK only when G1 can't keep up (compaction)

  ZGC / Shenandoah: almost all work concurrent → sub-ms pauses
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Minor vs Major vs Full vs G1 Mixed ═══

  Type        Scope              Cost        Collector notes
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Minor/Young Young gen only     cheap, ms   fires when Eden full
  Major       Old gen            costly      classic term; ≈Full in old GCs
  Full        whole heap+Meta    costliest   STW, pause ∝ live set
  G1 Mixed    young + few old    moderate    incremental old reclaim
  G1 Full     whole heap         rare        FALLBACK only (misconfig signal)

  Why G1 has no real "Major GC":
    - heap split into ~2048 regions (E/S/O/Humongous)
    - concurrent marking finds garbage-rich old regions (no STW)
    - mixed collections clean a FEW old regions per young pause
    - "Garbage First" = pick regions with most garbage per unit work
    → old reclamation is incremental, not one monolithic phase

  Classifier contract:
    name has Young/Scavenge/ParNew/Copy → MINOR bucket
    else → MAJOR/FULL/mixed bucket
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The three terms describe collections of different scope. A Minor GC collects only the Young generation, meaning Eden and the Survivor spaces, and it fires whenever Eden fills. It is cheap because its cost is proportional to the small number of surviving young objects, and although it is usually stop-the-world, the pause is typically only milliseconds, so a busy banking service can do many Minor GCs per second with negligible impact. A Major GC, in the classic vocabulary of the older collectors, refers to a collection of the Old generation, where long-lived tenured objects live, and it is far more expensive because the Old generation is larger and its objects are mostly still alive, so more of them must be traced and often compacted. A Full GC collects the entire heap, both generations, and usually unloads classes from Metaspace too, so it is the broadest and most expensive event.

The practical confusion I always clear up is that in the classic collectors, collecting the Old generation generally required a stop-the-world pass over the whole heap, so a Major GC and a Full GC looked nearly identical and the terms got used interchangeably. Strictly speaking, Major means the old space and Full means everything, but on those older collectors the distinction barely mattered in practice.

G1, the Garbage First collector and the default since Java 9, changes this model fundamentally, and that is why people say it does not really have a Major GC. Instead of two large contiguous generations, G1 divides the heap into a couple of thousand equal-sized regions, each labeled at any moment as Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous. Young collections evacuate the young regions just like a Minor GC. But for old garbage, G1 does not run one giant Major GC. It runs a concurrent marking cycle, mostly without stopping the application, to find which old regions hold the most garbage, and then it performs mixed collections, which are young collections that also evacuate a few of the most garbage-rich old regions at the same time. Because it only ever cleans the regions that give the most free space for the least work, old reclamation is spread across many short pauses rather than concentrated into one long one, which is exactly the Garbage First idea.

So there is no single dedicated stop-the-world phase in G1 that collects the whole Old generation at once. A true Full GC still exists in G1, but only as a rare fallback when G1 cannot keep up, for instance when the allocation rate outruns concurrent marking and the heap fills before mixed collections free enough space, and that fallback is a slow whole-heap compaction treated as a sign of misconfiguration. The senior point I close on is that modern collectors push this further still: ZGC and Shenandoah do essentially all of their work, including compaction, concurrently with the application, so they keep pauses in the sub-millisecond to low-single-digit-millisecond range even on very large heaps. For a balanced default I use G1, and for a large-heap, latency-critical banking service I would seriously evaluate ZGC.

---

keyPoints: Minor GC: Young Gen only — fast, frequent, low pause
Major GC: Old Gen only — slower, less frequent
Full GC: entire heap + metaspace — longest pause, most disruptive
G1 does not have a traditional Major GC — it does mixed collections
